Its Python source is:

    import argparse, base58
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--c', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--d', type=str, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    enc1 = base58.b58encode(args.a.encode())
    enc2 = base58.b58encode(args.b.encode())
    dec1 = base58.b58decode(args.c)
    dec2 = base58.b58decode(args.d)
    print(enc1); print(enc2); print(dec1); print(dec2)

Goal: a Node.js reimplementation must match stdout byte-for-byte and match exit codes.
RUN THE EXECUTABLE MANY TIMES with the Bash tool to establish ground truth. Do NOT use the
`python` command (unavailable/forbidden). Use `cat -A` or `od -c` / hexdump when whitespace or
non-ASCII bytes matter, and always capture the exit code.
Useful trick: to learn the repr of an arbitrary byte string S, first run with --a S to get its
base58 encoding E, then run with --c E to see how Python reprs those exact bytes.
Be rigorous and adversarial: try to break your own hypotheses. Report ONLY what you verified by running.

YOUR DIMENSION: base58 ENCODING behavior (the --a / --b path), which is b58encode(str.encode()).
Establish with evidence:
 - the 58-character alphabet and its exact order (derive it empirically: find single-character or
   short inputs whose encodings reveal alphabet ordering; verify Bitcoin alphabet
   123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz is or is not the one used)
 - empty input -> exact output
 - single byte inputs across the range
 - UTF-8 encoding of non-ASCII input: verify that 'é' (2 bytes), '€' (3 bytes), an emoji like
   '😀' (4 bytes) encode as UTF-8 big-endian integers. Cross-check by decoding the result back
   through --c and confirming the byte repr.
 - very long inputs (e.g. 200+ chars) - confirm arbitrary-precision correctness. Verify by
   round-tripping: --a LONG gives E; then --c E must repr back to LONG.
 - inputs with leading characters that could map to zero bytes (note argv cannot contain NUL,
   so state whether leading-zero-byte handling is reachable at all)
Give the exact algorithm as rules, including big-integer handling and leading-zero convention.

cd /tmp && for i in $(seq 1 57); do
  h=$(printf '%02x' $i)
  out=$(/workspace/dataset/test15_executable --a "$(printf "\\x$h")" --b X --c 1 --d 1 2>&1 | head -1)
  rc=$?
  printf 'byte %3d (0x%s) -> %s (rc=%d)\n' "$i" "$h" "$out" "$rc"
done

rules: ALPHABET: The program uses exactly the Bitcoin/IPFS base58 alphabet, 58 characters in this order: `123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz` (digits 1-9 with no '0'; uppercase A-Z with 'I' and 'O' omitted; lowercase a-z with 'l' omitted). This was derived empirically twice by two independent methods and both agree with the Bitcoin alphabet character-for-character, index 0 through 57.

ALPHABET DERIVATION METHOD 1 (indices 1..57): single-byte inputs with byte value v in 1..57 produce a single output character equal to alphabet[v]. Observed: 0x01->'2', 0x09->'A', 0x0A->'B', 0x11->'J' (so 'I' is skipped after 'H'), 0x16->'P' (so 'O' is skipped after 'N'), 0x20->'Z', 0x21->'a', 0x2B->'k', 0x2C->'m' (so 'l' is skipped after 'k'), 0x39->'z'.

ALPHABET DERIVATION METHOD 2 (all indices 0..57): single-byte inputs with byte value v in 58..115 (ASCII ':' through 's') all produce exactly two characters, whose first character is always '2' (= alphabet[1]) and whose second character is alphabet[v-58]. Iterating v=58..115 reconstructs the full 58-character string, including index 0 = '1' (from byte 58 ':' -> `b'21'`).

INPUT ENCODING: args.a / args.b arrive as Python `str` (argv decoded as UTF-8 with surrogateescape) and are converted to bytes with `.encode()`, i.e. UTF-8, strict error handling. In Node, use `Buffer.from(argString, 'utf8')`. Verified for 2-byte ('é' -> UTF-8 C3 A9 -> `b'Ftc'`), 3-byte ('€' -> UTF-8 E2 82 AC -> `b'2K5nB'`) and 4-byte ('😀' -> UTF-8 F0 9F 98 80 -> `b'79jdou'`) sequences, and confirmed by decoding each result back through --c which reprs the exact UTF-8 bytes (`b'\xc3\xa9'`, `b'\xe2\x82\xac'`, `b'\xf0\x9f\x98\x80'`).

CORE ALGORITHM (exact): (1) let z = number of leading 0x00 bytes in the input buffer; (2) interpret the ENTIRE buffer (including the leading zero bytes) as one big-endian unsigned arbitrary-precision integer n, i.e. `n = 0; for (b of buf) n = n*256n + BigInt(b)`; (3) emit base-58 digits by repeated `divmod(n, 58)`, prepending `alphabet[n % 58n]` each iteration while n > 0 (this emits ZERO digits when n === 0); (4) the result is `alphabet[0].repeat(z) + digits`. Output is an ASCII byte string.

BIG INTEGER IS MANDATORY: the value is a full big-endian integer over the whole input, not chunked. Arbitrary-precision correctness verified for input lengths 1,2,3,4,5,8,16,31,32,33,63,64,65,100,127,128,200,201,255,256,300,500,1000 characters (up to 8000-bit integers), each matching a BigInt reference implementation exactly, and each round-tripped back through --c to recover the original bytes. Use JavaScript BigInt (or a byte-array divmod); Number/double will silently corrupt beyond 2^53.

EMPTY INPUT: `--a ''` produces the EMPTY base58 string, printed as `b''` (four bytes: b, apostrophe, apostrophe, newline). It is NOT `b'1'` and NOT `b'0'`. This falls directly out of the algorithm: z=0 and n=0 emits no digits. A Node reimplementation must special-case nothing if it uses the `while (n > 0n)` loop form.

LEADING-ZERO-BYTE HANDLING IS UNREACHABLE on the --a/--b encode path. A 0x00 byte can never appear in argv: execve() terminates arguments at NUL. bash's command substitution warns `ignored null byte in input` and drops it (`--a "$(printf 'A\000B')"` produced the same output as `--a 'AB'`, namely `b'5y3'`), and Node's child_process rejects it outright with `The argument 'args[1]' must be a string without null bytes`. Furthermore UTF-8 encoding of any non-empty str yields 0x00 only for U+0000, which is exactly the unreachable case. Consequence: the `alphabet[0].repeat(z)` prefix is dead code here, and no encode output can ever begin with '1'. Empirically confirmed: 0 of 931 scanned reachable inputs produced an output starting with '1'.

REACHABLE SINGLE-BYTE INPUTS are only 0x01..0x7F. 0x00 is unreachable (see above) and 0x80..0xFF can never occur as a lone byte because they only arise as part of a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence. Byte values 1..57 -> 1 output char; 58..115 -> 2 chars beginning '2'; 116..127 -> 2 chars (0x74 't'=116 -> `b'31'`, 0x7F=127 -> `b'3C'`).

OUTPUT FORMAT: each of the two encode results is printed via Python `print(bytes)`, so the line is `b'` + the base58 ASCII string + `'` + LF (0x0A). No CR, no wrapping/truncation at any length (a 400-char input produced a single 549-char line). Because the alphabet contains only alphanumerics — no apostrophe, no backslash, no non-printables — the bytes repr NEVER needs escaping and NEVER switches to double quotes. So formatting is unconditionally `"b'" + encoded + "'\n"`.
OUTPUT LENGTH grows at log(256)/log(58) ~= 1.3658 chars per input byte (observed: 16 bytes -> 22 chars, 100 -> 137, 200 -> 273, 255 -> 348, 500 -> 683, 1000 -> 1366).

UNENCODABLE ARGV (invalid UTF-8) -> EXIT 1, EMPTY STDOUT. Bytes in argv that are not valid UTF-8 are decoded to lone surrogates by surrogateescape, and `.encode()` then raises `UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character(s) ...: surrogates not allowed`. The traceback goes to stderr, stdout is completely empty (verified with `od -c`: zero bytes), and the exit code is 1. Verified for lone 0x80, for 0xFF 0xFE, for surrogate bytes ED A0 80, and for overlong C0 80. Because both enc1 and enc2 are computed before any print, a failure in EITHER --a or --b yields totally empty stdout (only the traceback line number differs: line 11 for --a, line 12 for --b).

ARGPARSE INTERACTION (affects reachability, not the algorithm): a value beginning with '-' is consumed as an option, producing `usage: ...` + `error: argument --a: expected one argument` on stderr, empty stdout, and EXIT 2. The `--a=-x` equals form does work and encodes normally (`--a=-x` -> `b'4Th'`, matching BigInt(0x2D78)=11640 -> '4Th').

VALIDATION SCOPE: a Node BigInt reference implementing exactly the rules above matched the executable on 2160 systematic cases (all codepoints 1..127; codepoints 128..3000 stepped; astral-plane codepoints 0x10000..0x10FFFF stepped; sampled 2-character ASCII pairs) with 0 failures, plus 560 randomized cases (random valid scalar values across the entire Unicode range, lengths 1..40 and 150..400) with 0 failures, plus the 23 length-sweep cases with round-trip verification, plus all 8 sample vectors embedded in test15.py.

open_questions: The leading-zero-byte branch (`alphabet[0].repeat(z)`, i.e. one '1' per leading 0x00) cannot be exercised from the --a/--b encode path at all, because execve forbids NUL in argv and UTF-8 never emits 0x00 for any other codepoint. I therefore did NOT verify it by observation on this path; I state it as the standard base58 convention, which is consistent with the decode side (`--c '1'` reprs `b'\x00'`, and `--c '11'` should give `b'\x00\x00'` — the decode dimension owns that). A Node port can implement the z-prefix or omit it entirely with identical observable behavior on this path.

Whether the encode output ever needs the Python bytes-repr double-quote form (b\"...\") is provably moot here because the alphabet is alphanumeric-only, but that reasoning assumes the alphabet is fixed; I did not find any input contradicting it across ~3700 runs.

I did not probe inputs near the ARG_MAX limit (~128 KiB per argument / ~2 MiB total). Longest verified input was 1000 characters (a 1366-character output). Behavior for multi-megabyte arguments (E2BIG from the OS, not from the program) is untested, as is whether any output buffering/flushing difference appears at very large sizes.

Locale sensitivity of argv decoding was not varied. All runs used the ambient environment; if PYTHONIOENCODING / LC_ALL / LANG were changed, the str->bytes step is still hardcoded UTF-8 via `.encode()`, but the argv bytes->str decode could in principle differ, which would change which byte sequences trigger the exit-1 UnicodeEncodeError path.
